claim: Typhoid toxin is an essential virulence factor for Salmonella Typhi, the cause of typhoid fever in humans.
source: Typhoid toxin is an essential virulence factor for Salmonella Typhi, the cause of typhoid fever in humans.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about S. Typhi and typhoid fever.

claim: Typhoid toxin is produced by Salmonella Typhi only when located within host cells.
source: This toxin has an unusual biology in that it is produced by Salmonella Typhi only when located within host cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Once synthesized, typhoid toxin is secreted to the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole.
source: Once synthesized, the toxin is secreted to the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole from where it is transported to the extracellular space by vesicle carrier intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Typhoid toxin is transported to the extracellular space by vesicle carrier intermediates.
source: Once synthesized, the toxin is secreted to the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole from where it is transported to the extracellular space by vesicle carrier intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor serves as typhoid toxin sorting receptor.
source: We found that the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor serves as typhoid toxin sorting receptor and that the coat protein COPII and the GTPase Sar1 mediate its packaging into vesicle carriers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including affinity purification, mass spectrometry, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The coat protein COPII mediates typhoid toxin packaging into vesicle carriers.
source: We found that the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor serves as typhoid toxin sorting receptor and that the coat protein COPII and the GTPase Sar1 mediate its packaging into vesicle carriers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments with SEC23B-deficient cells shown in Figure 4.

claim: The GTPase Sar1 mediates typhoid toxin packaging into vesicle carriers.
source: We found that the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor serves as typhoid toxin sorting receptor and that the coat protein COPII and the GTPase Sar1 mediate its packaging into vesicle carriers.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments with SAR1B-deficient cells shown in Figure 4.

claim: Formation of typhoid toxin carriers requires the specific environment of the Salmonella Typhi-containing vacuole.
source: Formation of the typhoid toxin carriers requires the specific environment of the Salmonella Typhi-containing vacuole, which is determined by the activities of specific effectors of its type III protein secretion systems.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing differences between S. Typhi and S. Typhimurium vacuoles and the effects of expressing S. Typhimurium effectors in S. Typhi, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: The environment of the Salmonella Typhi-containing vacuole is determined by the activities of specific effectors of its type III protein secretion systems.
source: Formation of the typhoid toxin carriers requires the specific environment of the Salmonella Typhi-containing vacuole, which is determined by the activities of specific effectors of its type III protein secretion systems.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with various type III secretion system effectors shown in Figure 3.

claim: Rab11B controls the intracellular transport of typhoid toxin carriers.
source: We also found that Rab11B and its interacting protein Rip11 control the intracellular transport of the typhoid toxin carriers, and the SNARE proteins VAMP7, SNAP23, and Syntaxin 4 their fusion to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with Rab11B-deficient cells shown in Figure 5.

claim: Rip11 controls the intracellular transport of typhoid toxin carriers.
source: We also found that Rab11B and its interacting protein Rip11 control the intracellular transport of the typhoid toxin carriers, and the SNARE proteins VAMP7, SNAP23, and Syntaxin 4 their fusion to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with Rip11-deficient cells shown in Figure 5.

claim: VAMP7 mediates fusion of typhoid toxin carriers to the plasma membrane.
source: We also found that Rab11B and its interacting protein Rip11 control the intracellular transport of the typhoid toxin carriers, and the SNARE proteins VAMP7, SNAP23, and Syntaxin 4 their fusion to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with VAMP7-deficient cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: SNAP23 mediates fusion of typhoid toxin carriers to the plasma membrane.
source: We also found that Rab11B and its interacting protein Rip11 control the intracellular transport of the typhoid toxin carriers, and the SNARE proteins VAMP7, SNAP23, and Syntaxin 4 their fusion to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with SNAP23-deficient cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: Syntaxin 4 mediates fusion of typhoid toxin carriers to the plasma membrane.
source: We also found that Rab11B and its interacting protein Rip11 control the intracellular transport of the typhoid toxin carriers, and the SNARE proteins VAMP7, SNAP23, and Syntaxin 4 their fusion to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with STX4-deficient cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: Typhoid fever affects approximately 20 million people every year.
source: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi is the cause of typhoid fever in humans, a systemic disease that affects approximately 20 million people every year resulting in approximately 150,000 deaths worldwide (Buckle et al., 2012; Dougan and Baker, 2014; Kim et al., 2017; Mogasale et al., 2014; Parry et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Typhoid fever results in approximately 150,000 deaths worldwide annually.
source: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi is the cause of typhoid fever in humans, a systemic disease that affects approximately 20 million people every year resulting in approximately 150,000 deaths worldwide (Buckle et al., 2012; Dougan and Baker, 2014; Kim et al., 2017; Mogasale et al., 2014; Parry et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: S. enterica serovar Paratyphi A causes paratyphoid fever in humans.
source: A related pathogen, S. enterica serovar Paratyphi A, causes a very similar disease in humans (paratyphoid fever) and is increasingly becoming more prevalent in certain areas of the world.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about S. Paratyphi A.

claim: S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A are restricted to the human host.
source: Both serovars are restricted to the human host and no animal reservoir for these pathogens has been identified.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the host specificity of these pathogens.

claim: Multiple-antibiotic resistant strains of S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A are becoming endemic in different parts of the world.
source: The emergence of multiple-antibiotic resistant strains of these pathogens, which are becoming endemic in different parts of the world, is a major concern as it is complicating the available therapies (Chau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on antibiotic resistance.

claim: There are no vaccines available for S. Paratyphi A.
source: Although there are several vaccines available that confer partial protection to S. Typhi infection, there are no vaccines available for S. Paratyphi A (Milligan et al., 2018; Zuckerman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to vaccine studies.

claim: Typhoid toxin is encoded by both S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A.
source: Typhoid toxin is a virulence factor that is encoded by both, S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A, but that is largely absent from other S. enterica serovars that cause self-limiting gastroenteritis (i.e. non-typhoidal serovars) (Fowler and Galán, 2018; Fowler, 2019; Galán, 2016; Haghjoo and Galán, 2004; Song et al., 2013; Spanò et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on typhoid toxin.

claim: Typhoid toxin is largely absent from non-typhoidal S. enterica serovars.
source: Typhoid toxin is a virulence factor that is encoded by both, S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A, but that is largely absent from other S. enterica serovars that cause self-limiting gastroenteritis (i.e. non-typhoidal serovars) (Fowler and Galán, 2018; Fowler, 2019; Galán, 2016; Haghjoo and Galán, 2004; Song et al., 2013; Spanò et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on typhoid toxin distribution.

claim: Typhoid toxin has two covalently linked A subunits (PltA and CdtB).
source: Rather than one enzymatic 'A' subunit as seen in all other AB5 toxins, typhoid toxin has two covalently linked A subunits (PltA and CdtB) linked to a pentameric 'B' subunit alternatively composed of PltB or PltC (Fowler, 2019; Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of typhoid toxin.

claim: PltA is an ADP-ribosyl transferase with an unknown cellular target.
source: PltA is an ADP-ribosyl transferase with an unknown cellular target, and CdtB is an atypical deoxyribonuclease, which inflicts DNA damage on the intoxicated cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic activities of typhoid toxin subunits.

claim: CdtB is an atypical deoxyribonuclease that inflicts DNA damage on intoxicated cells.
source: PltA is an ADP-ribosyl transferase with an unknown cellular target, and CdtB is an atypical deoxyribonuclease, which inflicts DNA damage on the intoxicated cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic activities of typhoid toxin subunits.

claim: The PltB subunit of typhoid toxin specifically recognizes acetyl neuraminic acid (Neu5Ac)-terminated sialoglycans.
source: Consistent with the human host specificity of both, S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A, the PltB subunit of typhoid toxin specifically recognizes acetyl neuraminic acid (Neu5Ac)-terminated sialoglycans, which are almost unique to the human host since most other mammals display glycolyl neuraminic acid (Neu5Gc)-terminated glycans (Deng et al., 2014; Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on toxin-receptor interactions.

claim: Neu5Ac-terminated sialoglycans are almost unique to the human host.
source: Consistent with the human host specificity of both, S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A, the PltB subunit of typhoid toxin specifically recognizes acetyl neuraminic acid (Neu5Ac)-terminated sialoglycans, which are almost unique to the human host since most other mammals display glycolyl neuraminic acid (Neu5Gc)-terminated glycans (Deng et al., 2014; Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on sialic acid biology.

claim: Typhoid toxin does not appear to be required for the initiation of S. Typhi infection in humans.
source: A human volunteer study suggested that typhoid toxin does not appear to be required for the initiation of S. Typhi infection (Gibani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a human volunteer study.

claim: Administration of typhoid toxin into animals engineered to display Neu5Ac-terminated sialoglycans reproduced many symptoms of severe typhoid.
source: However, administration of typhoid toxin into animals engineered to display Neu5Ac-terminated sialoglycans reproduced many of the symptoms of severe typhoid, including various neurological symptoms, stupor, and profound leukopenia (Deng et al., 2014; Fowler, 2019; Song et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2018), aspects of the disease that for ethical reasons could not be captured in the human volunteer study (Gibani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: Typhoid toxin is secreted from bacteria to the lumen of the SCV through a novel dedicated protein secretion system.
source: Once produced, the toxin is secreted from the bacteria to the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole (SCV) through a novel dedicated protein secretion system (Geiger et al., 2020; Geiger et al., 2018; Hodak and Galán, 2012), which has been recently proposed to be classified as type X (Palmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the toxin secretion system.

claim: The typhoid toxin secretion system has been proposed to be classified as type X.
source: Once produced, the toxin is secreted from the bacteria to the lumen of the Salmonella-containing vacuole (SCV) through a novel dedicated protein secretion system (Geiger et al., 2020; Geiger et al., 2018; Hodak and Galán, 2012), which has been recently proposed to be classified as type X (Palmer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a classification proposal.

claim: Typhoid toxin is packaged within vesicle carriers that transport it to the extracellular space.
source: The toxin is then packaged within vesicle carriers, which transport it to the extracellular space (Chang et al., 2016; Spanò and Galán, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: After receptor-mediated endocytosis, typhoid toxin is transported to its intracellular destination via a specialized retrograde transport pathway.
source: The toxin then binds its specific Neu5Ac-bearing receptors, and after receptor-mediated endocytosis, it is transported to its intracellular destination via a specialized retrograde transport pathway (Chang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on toxin trafficking.

claim: There is no pathway that can transport typhoid toxin from the SCV to its place of action within the same cell.
source: There is no pathway that can transport the toxin from its site of production within the SCV to its place of action within the same cell and therefore intoxication always requires the export of the toxin to the extracellular space (Spanò et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and logical inference about toxin biology.

claim: A single amino acid substitution in the glycan-binding site of PltB (PltBS35A) results in a toxin that remains trapped within the SCV.
source: A single amino acid substitution in the glycan-binding site of PltB results in a toxin that remains trapped within the SCV after its secretion from the bacteria (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Toxin export requires a sorting event mediated by a glycosylated receptor on the luminal side of the S. Typhi-containing vacuolar membrane.
source: This observation suggests that toxin export requires a sorting event most likely mediated by a glycosylated receptor on the luminal side of the S. Typhi-containing vacuolar membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation about the PltBS35A mutant.

claim: CI-M6PR was identified as a prominent interacting protein with wild-type typhoid toxin but not with its PltBS35A mutant.
source: The cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor (CI-M6PR) (Gary-Bobo et al., 2007; Stalder and Gershlick, 2020) was identified as a prominent interacting protein with wild-type typhoid toxin but not with its PltBS35A mutant control (Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from affinity purification and mass spectrometry shown in Figure 1.

claim: CI-M6PR interacts with wild-type typhoid toxin but not with the PltBS35A mutant in S. Typhi-infected cells.
source: Similar to the in vitro experiments, we detected the interaction of CI-M6PR with wild-type typhoid toxin but not with the PltBS35A mutant version (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: CI-M6PR is recruited to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole, particularly later in infection.
source: Consistent with these observations, we found that CI-M6PR is recruited to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole, particularly later in infection (Figure 1c and d and Figure 1—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: Recruitment of CI-M6PR to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole was not due to its delivery to lysosomes.
source: Recruitment of CI-M6PR to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole was not due to its delivery to lysosomes since we did not detect the presence of the lysosomal hydrolases on the S. Typhi-containing vacuole (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CI-M6PR is not recruited to the vacuoles that contain S. Typhimurium.
source: These observations are intriguing since it is well established that CI-M6PR is not recruited to the vacuoles that contain S. Typhimurium (Garcia-del Portillo and Finlay, 1995; McGourty et al., 2012), which does not encode typhoid toxin.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Inactivation of CI-M6PR did not affect the ability of S. Typhi to gain access to and replicate within cells.
source: We found that inactivation of CI-M6PR did not affect the ability of S. Typhi to gain access to and replicate within these cells (Figure 2b and Figure 2—source data 2), neither it affected the ability of typhoid toxin to be internalized and intoxicate these cells when exogenously applied (Figure 2c and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial survival assays shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Inactivation of CI-M6PR did not affect the ability of typhoid toxin to be internalized and intoxicate cells when exogenously applied.
source: We found that inactivation of CI-M6PR did not affect the ability of S. Typhi to gain access to and replicate within these cells (Figure 2b and Figure 2—source data 2), neither it affected the ability of typhoid toxin to be internalized and intoxicate these cells when exogenously applied (Figure 2c and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by toxicity assays shown in Figure 2c.

claim: CI-M6PR-deficient cells show a marked reduction in the number of typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates.
source: We found in CI-M6PR-deficient cells relative to the parental cell line a marked reduction in the number of typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates that can be visualized as typhoid toxin-associated fluorescent puncta (Figure 2d and e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2d and e.

claim: CI-M6PR-deficient cells show reduced levels of typhoid toxin in the extracellular medium.
source: Consistent with a decreased formation of typhoid toxin carrier intermediates, we also found a reduced level of typhoid toxin in the extracellular medium of S. Typhi-infected CI-M6PR-deficient cells (Figure 2f–h, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by toxin export assays shown in Figure 2f-h.

claim: There was no evidence for extracellular protease activity that could account for reduced typhoid toxin levels in CI-M6PR-deficient cells.
source: However, we found no evidence for the presence of extracellular protease activity that could account for the reduced levels of typhoid toxin in the extracellular media of S. Typhi-infected CI-M6PR -/- cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by protease activity assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Rab29, Rab32, and Rab38 are robustly recruited to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole but are absent in the S. Typhimurium vacuole.
source: For example, while the Rab-family GTPases Rab29, Rab32, and Rab38 are robustly recruited to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole, these GTPases are absent in the vacuolar compartment harboring S. Typhimurium (Spanò and Galán, 2012; Spanò et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: S. Typhimurium prevents recruitment of Rab29, Rab32, and Rab38 by delivering effectors GtgE and SopD2.
source: Specifically, S. Typhimurium prevents the recruitment of Rab29, Rab32, and Rab38 by delivering of two effectors, GtgE and SopD2, which are absent from S. Typhi and target these Rab GTPases with specific protease and GAP activities, respectively (Spanò et al., 2016; Spanò et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The S. Typhimurium-containing vacuole does not recruit CI-M6PR due to the activity of type III-secreted effectors.
source: It is also well established that the S. Typhimurium-containing vacuole does not recruit CI-M6PR, and that the lack of recruitment of this lysosomal marker is also linked to the activity of type III-secreted effectors (McGourty et al., 2012; Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Typhoid toxin is not packaged into vesicle carrier intermediates when expressed in S. Typhimurium.
source: Cells infected with the S. Typhimurium strain expressing typhoid toxin showed markedly reduced levels of vesicle carrier intermediates when compared to S. Typhi-infected cells, despite equivalent levels of toxin expression (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Expression of SseJ in S. Typhi resulted in a significant reduction in the recruitment of CI-M6PR to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole.
source: Of all the effectors tested, only the expression of SseJ resulted in a significant reduction in the recruitment of CI-M6PR to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole (Figure 3c and d, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 3—source data 1), without altering the total levels of CI-M6PR in the infected cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: Expression of SseJ in S. Typhi significantly reduced the formation of typhoid toxin carriers.
source: Consistent with the reduced recruitment of its sorting receptor, the formation of the typhoid toxin carriers in cells infected with the SseJ-expressing S. Typhi strain was significantly reduced (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 7 and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: SseJ modifies the lipid composition of the SCV by esterifying cholesterol through its glycerophospholipid:cholesterol acyltransferase activity.
source: SseJ has been shown to modify the lipid composition of the SCV by esterifying cholesterol through its glycerophospholipid:cholesterol acyltransferase activity (Kolodziejek and Miller, 2015; Ohlson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Expression of catalytic mutant SseJS151A in S. Typhi had no effect on the recruitment of CI-M6PR to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole.
source: We found that in contrast to wild type, expression of SseJS151A had no effect in the recruitment of CI-M6PR to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole, and on the formation of typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 7, and Figure 3—source data 1), indicating that the modification of the lipid composition of the SCV through SseJ's catalytic activity influences CI-M6PR recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3e and supplements.

claim: The modification of the lipid composition of the SCV through SseJ's catalytic activity influences CI-M6PR recruitment.
source: We found that in contrast to wild type, expression of SseJS151A had no effect in the recruitment of CI-M6PR to the S. Typhi-containing vacuole, and on the formation of typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 7, and Figure 3—source data 1), indicating that the modification of the lipid composition of the SCV through SseJ's catalytic activity influences CI-M6PR recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of wild-type SseJ and the catalytic mutant.

claim: SEC23B-deficient cells showed a significant decrease in the formation of typhoid toxin carriers.
source: In contrast, SEC23B-deficient cells showed a significant decrease in the formation of typhoid toxin carriers and reduced toxin export (Figure 4b–d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and toxin export data shown in Figure 4b-d.

claim: SEC23B-deficient cells showed reduced typhoid toxin export.
source: In contrast, SEC23B-deficient cells showed a significant decrease in the formation of typhoid toxin carriers and reduced toxin export (Figure 4b–d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by toxin export assays shown in Figure 4c and d.

claim: Recruitment of CI-M6PR to the S. Typhi-containing vacuoles in SEC23B-deficient cells was indistinguishable from parental cells.
source: Recruitment of the packaging receptor CI-M6PR to the S. Typhi-containing vacuoles in SEC23B-deficient cells was indistinguishable from the recruitment observed in the parental cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 5—source data 1), indicating that the defect in typhoid toxin packaging was not due to the impaired recruitment of CI-M6PR.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: SAR1B-deficient cells showed a marked reduction in the levels of typhoid toxin carrier intermediates.
source: We found a marked reduction in the levels of fluorescent puncta associated with toxin carriers in SAR1B-deficient cells infected with S. Typhi despite similar expression levels of typhoid toxin (Figure 4e and f, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: SAR1B-deficient cells showed a significant decrease in the levels of typhoid toxin in the infection medium.
source: Consistent with this observation, in comparison to the parental cell line, we found a significant decrease in the levels of typhoid toxin in the infection medium of SAR1B-deficient cells (Figure 4g and h, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by toxin export assays shown in Figure 4g and h.

claim: Sec23 is robustly recruited to the SCV, particularly at later times after infection.
source: We observed robust recruitment of Sec23 to the SCV, particularly at later times after infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: Typhoid toxin forms a complex with SEC23 in HEK293T cells infected with wild-type S. Typhi.
source: We found that typhoid toxin could be detected in complex with SEC23 in HEK293T parental cells infected with wild-type S. Typhi (Figure 4i), although formation of the complex was markedly reduced in cells infected with the S. Typhi ∆spiA mutant strain (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Formation of the typhoid toxin-Sec23 complex was markedly reduced in cells infected with the S. Typhi ∆spiA mutant.
source: We found that typhoid toxin could be detected in complex with SEC23 in HEK293T parental cells infected with wild-type S. Typhi (Figure 4i), although formation of the complex was markedly reduced in cells infected with the S. Typhi ∆spiA mutant strain (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: The typhoid toxin-Sec23 complex could not be detected in cells lacking CI-M6PR.
source: Importantly, the typhoid toxin-Sec23 complex could not be detected in cells lacking CI-M6PR, indicating that formation of the complex requires the presence of the toxin's sorting receptor (Figure 4j).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Cells defective in Rab11B exhibited significantly reduced export of typhoid toxin to the extracellular media.
source: In contrast, cells defective in Rab11B (but not in its close homolog Rab11A) exhibited significantly reduced export of typhoid toxin to the extracellular media (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Figure 5—source data 1), even though the levels of toxin expression in the infected cells were indistinguishable from those of the parent cell (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by toxin export assays shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Rab11B-deficient cells showed normal levels of typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates.
source: Although the absence of Rab11B translated into a slight (not statistically significant) reduction in the immunofluorescence associated with typhoid toxin transport carriers (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, and Figure 5—source data 1), this difference cannot account for the observed differences in toxin export (Figure 5a and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Rip11-deficient cells showed a significant reduction in the export of typhoid toxin to the extracellular medium.
source: We found that the absence of Rip11 resulted in a significant reduction in the export of typhoid toxin to the extracellular medium relative to parental cell (Figure 5d and Figure 5—source data 1), despite equivalent levels of typhoid toxin expression (Figure 5e) and typhoid toxin carrier formation (Figure 5f, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—source data 1), a phenotype similar to that observed for the absence of Rab11B (Figure 5a–c and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by toxin export assays shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Rip11-deficient cells showed normal levels of typhoid toxin carrier formation.
source: We found that the absence of Rip11 resulted in a significant reduction in the export of typhoid toxin to the extracellular medium relative to parental cell (Figure 5d and Figure 5—source data 1), despite equivalent levels of typhoid toxin expression (Figure 5e) and typhoid toxin carrier formation (Figure 5f, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Figure 6—source data 1), a phenotype similar to that observed for the absence of Rab11B (Figure 5a–c and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: SNAP23-deficient cells showed significantly reduced levels of typhoid toxin in the infection media.
source: We found that the amount of typhoid toxin in the infection media of SNAP23-deficient cells was significantly reduced when compared to the parental cell line (Figure 6a and Figure 6—source data 1), despite equivalent amount of toxin expression (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by toxin export assays shown in Figure 6a.

claim: SNAP23-deficient cells showed increased levels of typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates.
source: In contrast, we found that the levels of typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates were actually increased in the SNAP23-deficient cells (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: STX4-deficient cells showed significantly reduced levels of typhoid toxin in the infection media.
source: We found that the level of typhoid toxin in the infection media of STX4-deficient cells was significantly reduced in comparison to the parental cell line (Figure 6a) despite equivalent levels of toxin expression (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by toxin export assays shown in Figure 6a.

claim: STX11-deficient cells showed increased typhoid toxin export.
source: In contrast, typhoid toxin export was increased in STX11-deficient cells (Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by toxin export assays shown in Figure 6a.

claim: STX4-deficient cells showed an increased amount of typhoid toxin carrier intermediates in the cytosol.
source: In addition, similar to SNAP23-deficient cells, we observed an increased amount of typhoid toxin carrier intermediates in the cytosol of STX4-deficient cells infected with S. Typhi (although the difference did not reach statistical significance), most likely due to the failure of these carriers to fuse with the plasma membrane (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: VAMP-7-deficient cells showed reduced typhoid toxin levels in the infection media.
source: Consistent with the involvement of VAMP-7 in typhoid toxin export, we found reduced toxin levels in the infection media of VAMP-7-deficient cells infected with S. Typhi (Figure 6a and Figure 6—source data 1), although the levels of typhoid toxin carrier intermediates were not significantly altered in these cells (Figure 6c and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by toxin export assays shown in Figure 6a.

claim: VAMP-7-deficient cells showed no significant alteration in the levels of typhoid toxin carrier intermediates.
source: Consistent with the involvement of VAMP-7 in typhoid toxin export, we found reduced toxin levels in the infection media of VAMP-7-deficient cells infected with S. Typhi (Figure 6a and Figure 6—source data 1), although the levels of typhoid toxin carrier intermediates were not significantly altered in these cells (Figure 6c and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The VAMP7/SNAP23/STX4 SNARE complex controls the last step in typhoid toxin export by targeting vesicle carriers for fusion to the plasma membrane.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the last step in typhoid toxin export is controlled by the VAMP7/SNAP23/STX4 SNARE complex, which targets the typhoid toxin vesicle carrier intermediates for fusion to the plasma membrane and subsequent release of the toxin cargo to the extracellular space.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from VAMP7, SNAP23, and STX4 knockout experiments.

claim: Typhoid toxin has coopted cellular machinery involved in various secretory and exocytic pathways.
source: The export pathway, which has evolved to be specifically adapted to the biology of Salmonella Typhi, has coopted cellular machinery involved in various secretory and exocytic pathways (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Rab11B has been shown to modulate the exocytic transport of insulin granules by linking transport carriers to kinesin motors.
source: This hypothesis is based on the observation that Rab11B has been shown to modulate the exocytic transport of insulin granules at least in part by linking these transport carriers to kinesin motors, a function that requires the Rab11B effector Rip11 (Sugawara et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Rab11B may be involved in the movement of typhoid toxin carriers along microtubule tracks.
source: However, we hypothesize that this GTPase may be involved in the movement of the typhoid toxin carriers along microtubule tracks.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of Rab11B and the experimental observations.

claim: The SNAP23/STX4 complex has been shown to interact with the v-SNARE VAMP-7.
source: The SNAP23/STX4 complex has been shown to interact with the v-SNARE VAMP-7 (Röhl et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2014), and we found here that cells defective in VAMP-7 showed reduced levels of typhoid toxin in the extracellular media.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Henle-407 cells and HEK293T cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum.
source: Human intestinal epithelial Henle-407 cells (obtained from the Roy Curtiss III collection in 1987) and HEK293T cells (from the American Type Culture Collection) were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing cell culture conditions.

claim: Cells were infected with S. Typhi or S. Typhimurium strains at a multiplicity of infections (MOI) of 30 or 10, respectively.

Typhimurium strains at a multiplicity of infections (MOI) of 30 or 10, respectively, in Hank's balanced salt solution, and then incubated with culture medium containing 100 µg/ml gentamicin for 1 hr to kill extracellular bacteria.
